utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Bjelica, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, one minor administrative matter. Some more translations have come in. I don't know whether they've been placed on Your Honours' Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see 12A, 12B, and a 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, 15 of course we referred to, but in the end it was not given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And indeed a significant part of 15 I notice has Latin as well. I'm afraid that I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, doctor's Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I'll proceed, if I may, with Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, could you turn to tab 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You obtained this report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why did you obtain this report?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report shows a lot about how members of the Muslim people prepared themselves in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the secession, how they armed themselves. It shows all of their plans, and it speaks about the crimes they committed, the killing of the member of a wedding party. It's an overview of the things that happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I assume that Mr. Josse is going to proceed with more preliminary questions in relation to this report prior to the witness proceeding to talk about its substance, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The first question now whether Mr. Bjelica obtained the report, he said he did. So your next question. At the same time, Mr. Margetts, of course the -- we would get to the content of the report of course within the understanding and within the limits of this case. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The report that seems to come from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, do you know who precisely was the author or were the authors of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia established a committee on collection of data on crimes against humanity and international law. I have a lot of information about war crimes and all the events in the former Yugoslavia, but I was more interested in the segments that are relative to our territory, to our parts. I don't know who members of the committee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, again I have to stop you. The question was whether you know who precisely was the author. It's not for you to guide us through the report. Mr. Josse will put questions to you and of course then you may explain everything to us. But please listen carefully to the -- to the questions put to you by Mr. Josse. Mr. Josse, I take it that this first answer has either been -- the first question has either been answered or whether you'd like to further explore who exactly within the government drafted the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have just said that you were interested in what it had to say about your locality. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant was to inform the Trial Chamber that it is not just the Serbs who were responsible for what happened and to show the Trial Chamber that the Muslims prepared themselves, that they committed crimes, and how they prepared for the war, what crimes they committed against the Serbian people. And what I was especially interested in was the topic of the Patriotic League because that unit was established -- or that paramilitary unit was established a year prior to the beginning of the conflict, and this document shows it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a specific example. At paragraph 2.6, we see reference to an incident which is well-known and which this Court has heard a lot about and that I'm sure we don't need to go into as such again. I take it what you know about this incident is only what you've read and have been told by other people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And based on the information that you have received, as far as you're concerned, is this an accurate assessment as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is accurate. I had an opportunity to talk to the priests who were also at the wedding and with son of Mr. Gadovic who is a priest somewhere in Germany. He visited the military cemetery and the church on Mount Romanija. That's when I spoke to him. The story -- his story was the same. That's why I'm saying that this is certainly accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so far as references in this document, not only have you read but you brought to The Hague is concerned, in relation to the Patriotic League, does it concur with what you've been told and learnt?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it concurs with that completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question covered the whole of the document, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, we are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not at 2.6 anymore?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct. Sorry. That part that deals with Muslim army, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just ask for a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D167, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D167. Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness mentioned the creation of this Patriotic League one year before the conflict. Could he give us some explanations on this and indications on this? Or if it's in the document, could he tell us exactly where -- what is said in this document regarding this issue and what he can add to this, the conditions surrounding the condition of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just assist Your Honour in one sense. It's -- chapter 1 of the document deals with the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the witness could maybe add what he knows. He said that he knew things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course, if I may respectfully say, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you answer the learned Judge's question, please, Mr. Bjelica. You've had a chance to read chapter 1. Indeed, as you've already told the Chamber, you brought -- you provided this document to the Defence. What do you know about the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the local level in 1991 we were aware of the fact that the Patriotic League was being formed. We had some intelligence, and people from the field informed us when things started getting pear-shaped in Bosnia and Herzegovina and when the conflict started and when some members of the Patriotic League already started speaking publicly about the Patriotic League, like Mr. Halilovic, like Mr. Bisic, who was the deputy minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the deputy minister of defence. He said that in 1991 before the conflict they had already established nine district staffs, 103 municipal staffs out of 109 municipalities, and that they already had between 90.000 and 100.000 members of the Patriotic League. At the proposal of Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I have a document to that effect from the newspapers that was published in -- for the Federation. The government had adopted an initiative showing that war veterans who were involved in the establishment of the Patriotic League in 1991 and who were its members are supposed to enjoy special benefits, and they published that in the paper Oslobodjenje, published on the 10th of May, 2003. I'm going to provide you with that newspaper. I have a date when this was published. It says here, amongst other things, that the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina two days ago recommended to the Federal Ministry of Defence to establish the criteria for issuing certificates, based on which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a minute because we've all got this, in fact, it's tab 5. I just want to check. Could we ask what you're referring to, Mr. Bjelica, at tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not the same thing. Just a moment, please, bear with me. This is a government document establishing the rights of the members of the Patriotic League. They -- in 2003, they fully legalised the fact and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina stands by this document, but the article in the newspapers just confirms all that and confirms what I've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please see that the witness has tab 5 in front of him and direct him to the B/C/S at the very end. No, no, Madam Usher, could you please look in tab 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I -- I didn't see this, but that's the same thing and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been copied and it has been translated so that we can -- yes, please, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, well could that now have a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For the Court's information, my intention was going to be to introduce that as the part of double pensions material which we're still working on. But I'm quite happy to introduce it in this way, bearing in mind the witness has alluded to it of his own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there anything else you would like to ask, Mr. Bjelica, to the question asked by the learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I have answered the Honourable Judge's question. If there's anything else for me to add, I'm at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to move on to different topic, please, Mr. Bjelica, and that is this: At the very beginning of your evidence this time yesterday, in response to a question about your background and your removal from your job with the Serb Sarajevo Assembly, you talked about your relationship with Radovan Karadzic. Firstly, in 1991/1992, the period of this indictment, how would you describe your relationship with Dr. Karadzic? How close to him were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't describe that relationship as a very close one. I was a member of the SDS and Radovan Karadzic was its president, and our relationship can follow the party hierarchy. I didn't know Mr. Karadzic. I did not have an occasion to see him until August 1990 when he arrived in Sokolac to the founding meeting of the Serbian Democratic Party. And after that I saw him several times before the beginning of the war. I was not a member of the Municipal Board. I was not the president of the Municipal Board, and I did not have any particular meetings with Mr. Karadzic because I did not have any position in the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about as the war progressed in 1993 onwards, did you become closer to him -- up until the end of the war, until the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not become any closer. That was out of the question. When I became a member of the Executive Board of the SDS and then when I became the president of the SDS for Sokolac, we had more frequent contact. But we talked about things that had to do with the party. That -- our relationship was nothing but that; it was just a party dialogue. We exchanged advice. I asked for his position as the president of our party, and also at the time he was the president of the republic. And this is what all of us did in the entire republic, and there was no other reasons for the two of us to become closer. I may have wished our relations to be a bit closer, but it was not possible. We were not of the same generation. We did not know each other. Our families never met. My family never saw Dr. Karadzic or his wife or their daughter, and we did not have any close relations. If you purport to be close to somebody, then you have to socialise with them, your families have to socialise, you have to go to the movies, to the theatre with them, then you can be close to somebody. Whoever says I was close to him, it's nonsense. But he was the president of the party and I respected him as such. I respect every president of my party. Radovan, while he was the president of my party, I respected him, and I respected Mr. Buha. And I -- after Mr. Buha I also respected Mr. Kalinic, and I also respected Mr. Cavic. I'm a party man and I only looked at the things through the party. I didn't join the party because of Karadzic and Buha, but I saw that their programme was close to my views and that that programme contained most of the interests and feelings of the people that I belonged to. That was the only reason why I joined the party, not because I was close to Karadzic or any other president. I hope I'm making myself clear. I suppose to Karadzic while he was the president of the party. All the party presidents are the same for me. Buha, Karadzic, Cavic, Kalinic because I am in this business because of the party, not because of the individuals in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would let you finish your answer, but could you please slow down a bit the speed because the interpreters -- you would also want that we get translated every single word you speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you refute any suggestion that you have been responsible or involved in hiding Mr. Karadzic, following his indictment. His having indicted, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. This was also established by the authorities and competent bodies. There were a lot of insinuations and allegations with that respect. Mr. Karadzic did not hide in 1998. He met with a number of people; he negotiated with them. As far as I know, representatives of some countries, institutions, came, offered him things, and Mr. Karadzic said when he left the position in 1996 and when he transferred his authorities to Mrs. Plavsic, who became the president of the republic, and Mr. Aleksa Buha, who became the president of the Serb Democratic Party, he said that he had had an arrangement or an agreement with the American administration, with Mr. Holbrooke, according to which he had to move from the political life. Mrs. Albright confirmed that in 1997 when she arrived in Banja Luka and when she conveyed this to Biljana Plavsic, and the media conveyed this message. Mrs. Albright says that Karadzic should leave Pale. He adhered to the arrangement that he had reached with the representatives of the international institutions that were involved in the preparations for the Dayton Accords. I don't know what happened next. Nobody ever asked me either to support or to fund Dr. Karadzic. I am not a member of any special units. I was never a member of any special units; I was never trained to do that. I never engaged in any martial arts. I am a family man. I am a responsible man. Nobody ever asked for me to participate in any such thing, nor would I ever do that. I would never participate in any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I am receiving information, Mr. Bjelica, that you are speaking too fast and important parts of your evidence are not being drawn to this Chamber's attention because you are speaking too fast. A moment ago in the answer that you gave, you were talking about Mr. Karadzic transferring his authority to Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Buha, and you described Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Buha's relationship at that time with Mr. Karadzic. What did you say about those two people's interrelationship with Mr. Karadzic? Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic transferred his authorities to Mrs. Plavsic, whom he probably deemed the person of his utmost trust. In 1996 he stood by her candidacy for the president of the republic. He was the one who put her up as the president of the republic. And at that moment he transferred his authorities to a member of the Main Board, Professor Dr. Aleksa Buha, in the party that he had chaired until the constitution of the new Assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party and until the appointment of a new president of the Serbian Democratic Party. That means that these positions that he had held he transferred on to these two people and he never even thought about anybody else who might fill those two positions. This is how it stayed, and Mr. Buha remained the president of the party until June or July, until St. Vitus Day 1998, and Mrs. Plavsic became president in 1996 and stayed in the position until 1998. She was the president of the republic. And I can add to this that a majority of the members of the Main Board at the time were against the candidacy of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic as president of the republic. Many opposed that even publicly. They wanted somebody else instead of Mrs. Plavsic. Mrs. Plavsic, whom many considered a hard-line Serb, a very extreme or even the most extreme member of the leadership of Republika Srpska. And those people wanted to see her as a member of the institutions of the Republika Srpska. Nobody wanted the position instead of Mrs. Plavsic. And finally Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik accepted to be the candidate for a president -- for the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if Mr. Krajisnik will understand when I say this, that nobody else but him wanted to do that, wanted to be a candidate for the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, it's only now that the translation -- the interpreters have translated. Could you perhaps look at your screen now and then and you see the text is moving. Wait until it stops because then the text is processed and translated for us and then you continue. So I would now stop until I see the text stopping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, an illustration of the difficulty is you have just said that Mr. Krajisnik accepted the candidacy as the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you say that? Because, as we know, at that time he was the candidate for the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a mistake. I said he accepted the candidacy for a member --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. It illustrates the problems with speaking too fast. I want to move back, please, to 1991, and I appreciate that you were not in a central position within the SDS at that time. It was only much later that you became involved in -- well, the Executive Committee and other positions. But how did you understand the SDS's division between the party and state organs in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Board of the SDS -- or maybe it was a different organ of the SDS - at any rate at one of these organs a political attitude was adopted that the holders of the highest offices, highest function, within the SDS, both at the local and the level of the republic, would not be nominated for certain state functions. The idea was to divide party functions from state political functions. This would not have been good for the party or for the state for that matter, to have two or more offices or functions in one person. Mr. Karadzic at the time was the president of the party but did not have any office. Mr. Rajko Dukic was the president of the Executive Board of the SDS of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. He, too, did not have any state function. As for the local level, Mr. Mirko Malovic, who was the president of the Municipal Board at Sokolac, which is the function that I occupied later on, neither he nor I had any state functions. The situation was the same at Pale. Mr. Vujacic was first -- is one such example, followed by Mr. Sarac. Neither of the two had any state functions. The situation was the same in Rogatica and in the majority of the municipalities which implemented the decisions of the Main Board of the SDS. Now, what I mean when I say that the decisions and attitudes were implemented, I want to say that the SDS was a democratic party. Anybody could say what they wanted and express all sorts of criticism. Anything could become a subject of debate. And finally, the decisions were reached by the majority, and those decisions were binding to all. There were of course individuals who would not implement all decisions, and it was probably a mistake, the fact that during a certain period of time they did not suffer any consequences, that there were no disciplinary sanctions within the party for those who failed to respect the positions so adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you some specific questions about Mr. Krajisnik. Briefly, it's right that you did not know him at all through the war period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no need for Mr. Josse to lead on -- in respect to matters like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute, Your Honour, in dealing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my question as well. Is there any information with the Office of the Prosecution that Mr. Bjelica had any contacts or that he knew Mr. Krajisnik during the war period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's substantial information we have that, given the office and the function that Mr. Bjelica occupied, he would have -- he was in a position to have substantial contacts. He was involved in specific transactions, which we would say Mr. Krajisnik, if not controlled, was a principal involved in those transactions. And, quite frankly, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that you think that there are good reasons. The question put to you comes down to whether -- when did you get to know Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got to know Mr. Krajisnik on an occasion in the National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that time we had a problem with the deputy, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us approximately when that was, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember, but I was a member of a delegation. I don't think that Mr. Krajisnik would have noticed me. I don't know whether he knew me at the time. I doubt that he knew me before 1992 because Mr. Simic and the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Tupajic, they could have contact with Mr. Krajisnik. Whether those contacts were really entertained or not, I don't know. But at any rate, before the war, I did not have any need to contact him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, please. One second. You say you "doubt whether he knew me before 1992." On from when do you think he would have known you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that it must have been at the time when they arrive in Pale. I don't remember exactly. It could have been from the month of May. What I know for sure is that since that fall, when Mr. Krajisnik was in Kikinda, we were often members of the same delegation, the president of the municipality and the president of the Municipal Board. There was from time to time a need for such a delegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say the fall, are you talking about the fall of 1992? That's the first year of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I better now understand the opposition against leading. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you first have a one-to-one conversation with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I ever had a one-to-one conversation with Mr. Krajisnik. No, I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How did you assess Mr. Krajisnik's authority and power in the Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly you're referring to, but whatever was necessary for a municipality at the time was the subject of our contacts with the president of the republic, the Main Board and the government. So everything went through the president of the municipality and the president of the Executive Board or the brigades towards the Main Staff. The coordinator, on behalf of the political structures of the Sokolac municipality who contacted with the Main Staff, was Mr. Milan Tupajic, and he was authorised for a while by the Municipal Board of the SDS to represent the SDS and to communicate with the Main Staff, if this was needed, because he was the president of the municipality. And we wanted to avoid any abuse on behalf of politicians. The politicians were not supposed to interfere with the affairs of the military, so that's how -- so that's what was done and how we operated. We did not have any special need to communicate with Mr. Krajisnik. It is beyond dispute that Mr. Krajisnik enjoyed respect of the entire membership of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about outside of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside SDS as well. In other political parties, too. And he was respected by other communities, other peoples. Many people consider Mr. Krajisnik to be a flexible man who obviously fights for the interests of his own people but does not -- but respects interests of other communities. And that is the reason why he was often exposed to criticism from certain members of the SDS. He was suspected by some of them that he may have become too close with the representatives of the Muslim and Croat communities in the Assembly, where he worked. And I know that in the Assembly - and this is what I learned from the media, what I saw in the media - in the Assembly they -- it was their custom to respect each other's religious holidays and pay each other a visit. So this was a custom in the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this mutual respect between different communities. And I believe that he really did his utmost to prevent a forcible destruction of institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was in favour of the principle of consensus and compromise, which had been agreed, but which was rejected by some. And he endeavoured until the very last moment to prevent the representatives of Muslims and Croats from acting too hastily in proclaiming or calling the referendum and proclaiming the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it was because of these constant endeavours to preserve peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina that Mr. Krajisnik enjoyed deep respect amongst the people and also the respect of other political parties. And I don't think that the representatives of Croats and Muslims could express any significant criticism of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you understand Mr. Krajisnik to be a member of an expanded Presidency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard the term "expanded Presidency." A Presidency surely existed; it was established on constitutional basis in Republika Srpska. And it was made up of the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic; and two vice-presidents, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Nikola Koljevic. There were no other members of the Presidency. This was the only legal -- the only body after the government and the National Assembly. Had anyone else been the member of the Presidency, we would have known that, we would have learned that through the sessions and through the media. Three -- there were three members of the Presidency: Karadzic, Koljevic, and Plavsic. Therefore, Mr. Krajisnik was not a member of a Presidency, of the Presidency, because it was made up of three members only.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask my learned friends, in the last 65 ter that I sent them at paragraph 6 there is some evidence that involves Mr. Krajisnik. Can I lead in relation to that? I ask my learned friend generally yesterday. I appreciate I'm asking him to scramble through his papers at the moment, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thank Mr. Josse for that. When I didn't have the document before me, I did consent to him leading, so I thank him for again giving me the opportunity to put our position, and we do object to leading in regard to anything involving Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you'll understand that the Chamber can give no ruling on this in such general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you at this moment are trying to find out what the temperature in terms of leading is. You know it. Mr. Margetts certainly remembers that I asked him yesterday not to be oversensitive and we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I sent this document to the Chamber, but I'm not asking for a ruling. I accept what my learned friend has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I want to ask you to describe slowly and clearly an instant involving a Muslim girl called Minka from Gorazde, who was in a military hospital in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a girl by the name of Minka. She had some health problems sometime in early 1992 and was transferred to the hospital in Sokolac because it was an emergency, and the military hospital in Sokolac at the time had very good physicians who used to work in the military hospital in Sarajevo, Dr. Tausan and Dr. Nakas, a Muslim who later on returned to Sarajevo and who established a military hospital there. As a result of the war activities and everything that was going on --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Slowly, please, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a result of the events taking place at the time, this little girl could not be transferred back to her parents in Gorazde. So she stayed there throughout 1992 and well into 1993. She spent her time playing with the children of the hospital staff who lived in the vicinity. And there was an occasion - this is something that became known to me only later on - but at any rate the father of a missing person from the area of Gorazde, I think this missing person -- actually, I'm sure that the name of this missing person was Srdjan Djeric and his father's name was Dobrosav. So the father could not obtain any information whatsoever about his son, whether his son was still alive or had been killed; and if so, if his body could -- his remains could be returned. Someone told him -- because he went around, he knocked at many doors to the ICRC, UNPROFOR, and so on and so forth. But could not find anything, could not find an answer. So someone told him that a child from the area of Podravanje was in this local hospital and he wanted to kidnap the child but was prevented in doing so. So the International Committee of the Red Cross contacted Mr. Krajisnik at the time, asking him to use his authority and his -- and the respect that he enjoyed, to do something, to transfer this child -- to return this child back home. Mr. Krajisnik never issued any orders, never told anyone that something had to be done. So he kindly asked that the issue be investigated and an exchange team from the Ministry of the Interior was established. I remember a person by the name of Sevo who was a member of this committee. So this transfer was organised and the little girl was taken back to her parents to the territory that she had left a year and a half before. She was safely transferred, taken back, to her parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Margetts, are you ready to start the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed in order to have the documents here we would be grateful if we could have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could have the break now. It's quite early because we had a start of half an hour later, and then of course I'm a bit concerned of getting into difficulties later with tapes, et cetera, because we have a session now of only 50 minutes and that could bring us to some trouble. How much time would you need to get the material here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, this will not be the first long break, but my colleagues, generous as they always are, suggested six to seven minutes. We'll adjourn and we'll re-start at 10.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Margetts, counsel for the Prosecution. May I specifically instruct you to carefully listen to the questions because you have a tendency of telling us a lot, even portions that are not specifically asked. Mr. Margetts is under some time restraints. So if you would go that way, he might interrupt you, but I'll keep tight control over it. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, yesterday you referred to an intercept of telephone conversation between yourself and Mr. Karadzic wherein you discussed a transaction regarding fuel. And at page 52 of yesterday's transcript and from line 21, regarding that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you're looking -- Mr. Margetts is referring to yesterday's session, so page 52 is not accessible to you. It's just for the information of the Judges and counsel where to find your testimony of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it -- regarding that transaction you stated that it did not take place, nothing came of it. And precisely what you said was this. You said: "I don't think anything came of this. It was never realised. This business was never realised. They were two cisterns full of fuel that had to be paid for. We weren't able to meet those requirements, so this was a business transaction that never went through." Then further on at page 53, line 10, you stated: "We didn't have the money to pay for that, and so this never materialised. This business transaction never went through."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, at this stage, Your Honours, I'd like to distribute the documents and I'd like to refer Mr. Bjelica to tab 36 of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not many witnesses to go anymore, but the Chamber would not have minded if it would have been on our tables already. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, perhaps in order to avoid whatever confusion, perhaps we should take back from Mr. Bjelica the other bundle, unless you would use and need it immediately, Mr. Margetts. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, that's tab 36 that we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bjelica, you'll see that this is a remittance advice that's on the right hand of your copy, the right-hand bottom, the word "Sokolac" appears and the date, 30 December 1991. The transferee is Boksit Milici, and the purpose of the remittance is payment for oil derivatives. And you'll see that the account owner is a Sokolac-based company and that the sum that is transferred to Boksit Milici is 1.1 million dinars. In fact, Mr. Bjelica, you did have the resources and did pay for the fuel, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What has this got to do with me? I apologise. The primary school, Slavisa Vajner Cica, based in Sokolac paid for this, not Romanija. Here it says: "By order of the account owners Slavisa Vajner primary school Sokolac," and they remitted money to Boksit Milici. They needed money for -- for the heating. And this has to do with them, with the primary school in Sokolac called Slavisa Vajner Cica. You can read it on this transfer note.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. The -- there was substantial discussion in your evidence yesterday relating to whether or not the person referred to in the 27 December 1991 intercept was either Mirko Krajisnik of Boksit or, alternatively, a chap by the name of Slavo Krajisnik, who worked with Branko Ostojic. The fact is that Mirko Krajisnik, working at the Sarajevo office of Boksit, procured oil for Romanija Petrol, and he offered your company substantial quantities of oil, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sure of that. I don't know. I don't know that he delivered anything. He worked in that company, but we did not obtain fuel from any company executives. I don't remember this. I never had any arrangement with Mirko, and I don't know what is the basis of your conclusion. Could you please explain. Could you please clarify. I'm not clear. Why are you saying this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The first thing is, Mr. Bjelica, you need to listen very carefully to my questions and you need to answer my questions and not to re-formulate them in your own words. So instead of talking about delivery of fuel, first of all answer my question about Mirko Krajisnik procuring oil and making it available and offering it to your company, Romanija Petrol. He did that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, did you understand the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- in your answer you said: Never oil was delivered in that way, whereas Mr. Margetts asked you whether it was ever offered. So apart from whether delivery finally would take place, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could refer to tab 2 of the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I think we have not yet given a number to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- previous tab which was --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 36, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would be P1149.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if a number could be given to tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, tab 2 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 2 would be P1152.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, you have before you a communication from Mirko Krajisnik, and you'll see on the second page that it's signed and stamped "Mirko Krajisnik, Boksit Sarajevo branch." I can refer you to the first page, you'll see that Mr. Krajisnik had 420.000 litres of fuel available at -- that he has stored in Zvornik on the 1st of April, 1992. And he says this. He says: "We have offered our buyers part of the quantity in the following fashion," and the fourth company listed is your company, Romanija Petrol. And he's offered you, who he describes as one of his buyers, 33.000 litres of fuel. That's the case, isn't it? Mr. Krajisnik procured oil and he regarded your company as one of his buyers.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can tell from this document that the gentleman from Boksit, joint stock company based in Milici, offered fuel, that they were in a position to offer 193.000 litres of fuel. To Sinekop, 6.000; to Autoprevoz, 66.000 litres; to Azbest Petrol, 28.000 litres; and to Romanija Petrol, 33.000 litres. This was their offer. I don't know whether this was ever implemented, maybe through Zoran Pantic. I don't think it was ever purchased but it had to be paid for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop you. The fact is we -- prior to presenting this document to you, there was some detailed discussion about the difference between offering and delivery, and it was clarified both by myself and by the Court what that difference was. It's now not useful for you having looked at this document to go through that again. So let's not reduce this to a farce whereby we're debating words; let's just answer the questions precisely as they're put. The fact is that this document is correct. Mirko Krajisnik offered you fuel and he regarded you as one of his buyers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not consider me one of his buyers. I represented a state company called Romanija Petrol. I don't remember this document, and this is nothing but an offer. Whether this was ever realised, I don't know, it is possible, but I don't believe that it ever was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm going to intervene here and I'm going to look very carefully to my own words. I said to the witness that you asked him whether it was ever offered, and then I added: "So apart from whether delivery finally would take place, yes or no," and then the witness said "no." And that could be well understood as a confirmation of that it was not delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour. We may need to listen to the translation of Your Honour's question. With respect, Your Honour's question was not grammatically correct in English at all. I'm sorry to have to say that. It simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem was it was no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I remember when Your Honour said it thinking to myself: That is not altogether clear. I decided not to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's -- Mr. Josse, I suggest at this moment that what I said, first of all, was not a question. And since my last line ended with "yes or no," that was not a question. That was whether or not. And then the "no" from the witness could be well understood as confirming - although I didn't ask him for it - that there had been no delivery, without expressing himself in any way as to the clarified question as whether there had been any offer. I would consider this not an explanation which would be unfavourable. I think it's a fair explanation and it would certainly be rather in favour than disfavourable to the -- to the witness and to the Defence. Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm saying is the "no" from the witness -- I understand the "no" from the witness, looking at my own language, not to be an answer to the question whether ever it was offered, but more or less echoing the last line -- my last line about delivery. I said whether -- I should have said: So apart whether delivery final would take place --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour's question was: Did delivery ever take place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I just tried to explain that an offer does not necessarily include that there was delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can I -- learned counsel for the Defence is moving perilously close to making submissions as to what the record records. And that's his -- we have a different view, and we are quite content on the basis of the record to move forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After consultation with my colleagues, the "no" of the witness is not understood my this Chamber as a "no" to a question whether it was ever offered. It is understood as a "no" to whether it was ever -- whether any oil was ever delivered -- was delivered. Is that -- does that satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll stay further out of it. I tried to clarify the matter. I've not been successful. I leave it to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not entirely sure I'm content with that explanation either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I leave it to the parties and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do -- I better understand it. You're not entirely happy, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's just that I thought maybe Your Honour in explaining it in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you -- I should have possibly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- possibly contradicted the previous view. If Your Honour could review the transcript, you stated that it was a no to whether it was delivered, wherein in fact the specific intent of Your Honour's question was to respond to my inquiry as to whether it was in fact an offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I think there was some confusion there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'll ask you this, Mr. Bjelica: Whilst you continued to contend that no fuel was delivered, you do concede that this document from Mirko Krajisnik accurately sets out that he did offer you fuel?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this document before. It was not addressed to me. It is possible that somebody offered fuel by phone, and then if the price was not adequate we never accepted the offer. This is just a letter to the marketing department of the Boksit DD company based in Milici, indicating that they had a certain quantity of fuel at their disposal and that they offered it to the aforementioned companies. And it was well-known whether these companies purchased the fuel, whether they were going to purchase, or not. I see this document for the first time. Everybody offered oil at the time, and we did purchase oil from any company that was duly registered, as this company was, and if the price was adequate. If we had purchased fuel based on this document, it would be nothing to -- nothing questionable --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. But your evidence to this Court is that as director of Romanija Petrol when at the start of April 1992 Mirko Krajisnik offered your company 33.000 litres of fuel, you had no idea that that offer was provided to your company. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I'd like to move on to another topic, and that is the issue of the Romanija Autonomous Region. In paragraph 2 of your statement which you signed and is being presented as Exhibit D160 to this Court, you stated that the first meeting of the SAO Romanija Assembly -- there's no need for you to find the statement, Mr. Bjelica. You'll recall this. You stated that the first meeting of the SAO Romanija Assembly occurred in September of 1991 and there were no further meetings of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could refer to tab 15. And, Your Honour, this already has an exhibit number, that is, P64A, P529, tab 466.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you see the document before you. That is the minutes of a meeting of the SAO Romanija Assembly of December 1991, and it's a fact that that body did meet again after September 1991, didn't it? And if it assists you, Mr. Bjelica, you'll see that you in fact attended this meeting and spoke at it. That's at the bottom of the third page of the document you have before you. Mr. Bjelica, apart from possibly reading your own remarks, there's no need for you to look at the full document; I won't be asking you questions about it. The question is very specific, it's the fact that the Assembly did meet again, it met in December 1991. Correct? Correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see now that it did. This was not an Assembly; this was just a consultation meeting. And based on this, one can conclude that it was a consultation meeting of the government in an extended composition, the government of SAO Romanija, with representatives of Vlasenica and Sekovici because at that time there was an initiative - I don't know who launched it actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, Mr. Bjelica, because already your comments are contradicting the terms of the document. Because if you look at paragraph 1, the first item on the agenda, it's the decision to appoint the SAO Romanija government. So it's not a meeting of the government in extended form. As is set out in the heading of the document, it's a meeting of the Assembly, and that Assembly appoints the government on that day. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this had been envisaged, and you can see here representatives of Sekovici and Vlasenica. What they had got to do with this meeting. This may have been the first session at which the government was appointed, and my intervention was only to ask what the purpose of the meeting was and who was it who was trying to hold this meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Bjelica. Mr. Bjelica --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have even left the meeting before its conclusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, before you started your evidence in response to the cross-examination, His Honour said I will be asking specific questions, and I will do that and I again ask you for specific answers. I'm going to ask you a simple question: Is this a meeting of the SAO Romanija Assembly that you attended, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, not only --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- in your statement you've given to this Court did you say that no meetings of the Assembly occurred after September 1991, but you failed to mention altogether the fact that there was a government of the SAO Romanija, and also - I'll ask you two questions here - a Crisis Staff of the SAO Romanija that met and functioned. That's correct, isn't it, that those two bodies met in 1992 and issued decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me about the government, whether it was established or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the question is - and forget about what Mr. Margetts said about what you failed to say - did a government of SAO Romanija meet and function in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. They may have met, but I don't know. It is possible. It is possible that there were meetings, but I was not a member of that government and I don't remember. It is possible. There may have been meetings, but, believe me, I can't remember. I was not in the government. There were consultation meetings between the leadership and others. Whether somebody thought that that was the government or a Crisis Staff, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the second question, apart from the government: Are you aware of a SAO Romanija Crisis Staff meeting and functioning in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. There were meetings of the leaderships from the territory of Romanija, presidents of the party, presidents of the Municipal Boards, presidents of the municipalities. I don't know what the name of those meetings was and whether they consider themselves a Crisis Staff. I know that there was a Crisis Staff in my municipality, and whether this was a Crisis Staff, another one, I really can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can refer to tab 16, if that could be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 16 would be P1153, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, if I could refer you to the article which appears in the right-hand column of the document before you, and it's the second from the bottom. And it's headed "announcement by the SAO Romanija Crisis Staff." And it's published in the publication Glas on the 5th of March, 1992. The announcement that the Crisis Staff of the SAO Romanija makes is this that: "The Serbian people have lost their confidence in the possibility of a political agreement with the Muslim people because with their attacks against innocent Serbs, even children, militant part of the Muslim people have torn the last leaks between our two peoples in the roughest manner." That is the case in SAO Romanija, isn't it, Mr. Bjelica, that by the 5th of March, 1992, the leaderships of SAO Romanija had lost confidence in the possibility of any political agreement with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this. I don't know who declared this or signed this, whether this was Mr. Drago Blagojevic or Nedeljko Djukic, I don't know. But at any rate, this was not discussed at any forum. This was an announcement of a personal kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Bjelica. You have to listen to my questions, and my question was specific. It was that the people, the Serb people of SAO Romanija had lost confidence in the possibility of a political agreement. Now, take your eyes away from the article and listen to the question and answer the question. They had lost confidence in the possibility of a political agreement with the Muslims, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, if I could move on. You can close the documents before you. In -- at paragraph 5 of the statement that you signed and handed up to the Court, Exhibit D160, you stated that Zoran Cvijetic set up the SAO Romanija MUP ministry on the 30th of March, 1992. However, prior to the 30th of March, 1992, in fact on the 20th of March, 1992, Cvijetic had taken command of the SAO Romanija police and he had dismissed all the Muslims. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Bjelica, please. Just if you could leave the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bjelica, if you want to consult any documents you have brought yourself, please address me. Tell me what kind of document you would like to consult and for what reason there's need to consult the document before answering the question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not necessary for me to look at the document to answer the question. But the establishment of this unit in the month of March, I just wanted to illustrate this with an example of an article from a Sarajevo-based paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, first of all, interested in your testimony, Mr. Bjelica, because this Chamber heard that a lot of publications appeared, some telling one truth, others telling another truth. So we are a bit cautious with documents. We first like to hear your answer to the question because you're hear to tell us what you know. Please proceed. So the -- perhaps, Mr. Margetts, you repeat the questions which were actually two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll make it one question, if that would be more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, on the 20th of March, 1992, Zoran Cvijetic dismissed all the Muslims from the SAO Romanija police, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the SAO Romanija police but from the police station in Sokolac. That is true, that they left. Only with respect to Sokolac, not with the entire region of Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, again Mr. Margetts is asking you whether Mr. Cvijetic fired them or what term did you use?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Dismissed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dismissed, yes. Whether they were dismissed. You say: "Yes, that's true, they left," which is not the same. Did they left because they decided they didn't want to stay there anymore, this police force, or did Mr. Cvijetic tell them that they had to leave? Do you know that? If so, please tell us; if not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the answer to this question. It is true that those days - I don't recall the exact date but it shouldn't be a problem - that Muslims in the Sokolac police station were told by the chief security station, Mr. Cvijetic, that they did not come to work any longer until the status of Serbs in the old town, Gorazde and other municipalities, is resolved because these had been dismissed by the chief of the police station where Muslims were. So it was under these conditions that they were dismissed. He told them not to come to work to Sokolac until this issue had been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could move on, Mr. Bjelica. At paragraph 12 of the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, before I commence this question, what time will we be having the break, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to now -- so we'll have another break. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this would be a suitable moment, because we have now -- we went on for approximately one and a half hours. So then if this would be a suitable moment, we'll have a break now and then we'd resume at 25 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Krajisnik, the Trial Chamber would like to address you regarding the procedure which has been adopted with respect to letters - you may remain seated - you sent to the Chamber. This procedure was prepared by the Judges in light of the submissions made by the Defence at the Rule 73 ter pre-Defence conference on the 6th of October, 2005, with reference to the transcript pages 17269 through 17271. During that period, Chamber received several letters from you. Some of the matters raised were properly addressed directly to the Chamber, while others were not. We now understand that you asked Mr. Josse to give an envelope to the Chamber on your behalf and that this was presented to the Legal Officer after the close of last Wednesday's session. We want to be sure that you understand how this and all other letters from you will be handled today and in the future. Matters that are not, generally speaking, properly addressed directly to the Judges by an accused who is represented through counsel are those matters which your counsel have been hired to handle on your behalf as well as matters that are within the jurisdiction of the Registry in the first instance. Other matters not falling within either of these categories may also not be within the competence of the Chamber to deal with, although questions of competence cannot be defined in the abstract. Your counsel will be able to advise you on the question of the Chamber's competence in relation to a particular matter. According to the adopted procedure, Mr. Krajisnik, your correspondence will first be given to the Registry. It will then be translated into English and sent to one of the Chamber's Legal Officers. The Legal Officer will review the contents of the letter for any matter which is appropriately addressed directly to the Judges. Following the review, if the letter contains a matter that is appropriately addressed to the Judges directly by you, the Legal Officer will retain the letter for consideration by the Chamber. In the alternative, if the letter does not contain a matter that is appropriately addressed to the Judges directly by you, the Legal Officer will return the letter to the Registry, which will, in turn, send the letter back to you, Mr. Krajisnik. In either case, depending on the contents of the letter, the Chamber may send a notification and translated copy of the letter to Defence counsel. This is the procedure. Now, as far as this specific letter was concerned, the Chamber has decided not to deal with it unduly formalistic -- yes, may I first finish and tell us what we have in mind, and then I give you an opportunity to respond to that. Mr. Krajisnik, the letter has been translated. We have not read it yet, but we were informed that it deals with an invitation the Chamber gave to, I think to the Defence, and that's usually you and counsel, to give further information on witness issues, witnesses who may have fear to appear before this Tribunal. The Chamber considers this a matter which would -- should be addressed through counsel. If it were only for the reason that if it would be filed, then of course decisions can be taken, otherwise part of the file is missing. So, therefore, it should have been appropriately addressed to the Chamber through counsel. At the same time, we're not going to be over formalistic on the matter. But before we ask our staff to give the letter to us, I'd like you to briefly consult with Mr. Josse - I don't know whether Mr. Josse is aware of the content of the letter - and specifically discuss with him briefly what the content is, whether Mr. Josse would prefer to have it filed officially, because that's the problem with these kind of letters, that they do not become a part of the file, and then please inform us. If you say: Mr. Josse may file this information at a later -- well, tomorrow or next week, in an other way but there's no problem the Chamber reading the letter already, we'll just read it and then we'll see how Mr. Josse would give a follow-up to it. But we'd very much like you to have at least one or two words with Mr. Josse before we read the letter. It could be -- that's also a possibility -- and that's why the Chamber is reluctant, in writing a letter not having seen by counsel, there's always -- even if it would be small, there's always a small risk that it could damage your position. I mean, you never know. Sometimes only when having studied the letter very carefully it could be not good for your position. And therefore we want to make sure that such a thing does not happen. If there is anything you would like to add, please do so at this moment; if not, please have one word with Mr. Josse - perhaps that's even possible when the witness comes in - and see whether Mr. Josse -- whether we could already receive that letter. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I wrote the letter because of my intervention before this Chamber, and you adopted a decision that certain documents should be advanced. I told this to my counsel, and they handed over this documentation. I will once again consult with Mr. Josse to see whether this should really be contained in the documents, but I wanted to make sure that you get it as soon as possible so that you can see for yourself that my remark in connection with the witness's was justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, I'm now addressing you. Are you satisfied with the situation and that you look at it -- have you seen the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I really need the translation. When I handed it over to the Legal Officer, I made it plain that we had not had it translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter or the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to mislead the Court, because Mr. Krajisnik had been good enough to discuss it with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And -- in fact, Mr. Sladojevic summarised the letter in part. I then consulted with Mr. Stewart, spoke to Mr. Krajisnik, and we decided, for reasons I'm not going to go into now, the best course of action was to do exactly what Mr. Krajisnik wanted and hand the letter to the Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But I really, really need to see the translation. I emphasised that when I handed the letter in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we read it or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before -- I couldn't possibly advise my client without seeing a full translation of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll first verify whether, apart from the letter, any of the documents attached to it are translated as well. They are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we'll consider what to do, but perhaps most likely -- I do understand your concerns. I also do understand that Mr. Krajisnik would like us to be informed as soon as possible. At this moment I think wisest would be to ascertain that apart from the letter that also the newspaper -- I take it that the relevant portion is well-marked of that newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Or I'm not sure that -- it's not, but Mr. Krajisnik is happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be important, unless the whole of the newspaper deals with the same matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. There's one -- in fact, I've just been told now that a portion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a portion. Yes. Because then, of course, it saves a lot of resources if Mr. Krajisnik would then point out what is the relevant portion of the newspaper, then -- I mean, under normal circumstances, as I said before, if it's a matter which should be -- that should not be directly -- or should not appropriately directly addressed to the Chamber, we'd send it back. Let's not, as I said before, be unduly formalistic. We'll see whether it can be translated. Mr. Josse, you'll then have a very short moment to discuss the matter once you have seen both the translation of the letter and the translation of the newspaper, and then you decide together with Mr. Krajisnik whether it should be filed in a formal way. Whether you would consider you could advise Mr. Krajisnik on whether this is a matter to be addressed directly to the Chamber. Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Although I don't quite follow why it needs to be a short period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course if you say -- Mr. Krajisnik sent the letter to the Court. I said we will not unduly formalistically deal with it, which opens the way of us reading the letter even before it was officially filed. We have to decide at a certain moment whether we give the letter back or whether we wait for your filing or whatever solution, and we don't want to wait with that, because the matter is important enough not to be pending for a long period of time. Because that's, I understand, Mr. Krajisnik, was your concern that we would be informed as soon as possible and, therefore, under those circumstances we'd like to know as soon as possible whether to give the letter back to you, whether it will be filed, or even in this case where we already decide that we would read the letter and not rely formalistically on the procedure just set out, although we will apply it in the future, that we will then read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may say on behalf of Mr. Krajisnik and myself, that is a fair summary of the situation, and it was time constraints as much as anything which led us to decide jointly that the best course was simply to hand the letter in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Time constraints on our part are the precise -- one of the precise difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the letter now will be given back to Mr. Krajisnik. He will indeed mark in the newspaper article exactly what is the relevant portion. Then we will receive it back. It will be translated. You will have an opportunity, Mr. Josse, again -- briefly in order to tell us what we are expected to do, and then we'll finalise the matter, either through a formal filing, either by reading the letter in this exceptional case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Josse and Mr. Krajisnik, it may be entirely clear to you that the Chamber is not the quickest way of getting translations. I do not -- I do not -- it did not come into my mind that that was your intention, but I just want to say that translations should be normally not asked from CLSS by the Chamber but by the Defence. And the Defence includes counsel and accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you for making that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, once the witness has been brought in again -- I see it's a limited portion. Madam Usher, could you please ask the security to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, they've been listening, Your Honour. So I think Your Honour simply needs to say "bring the witness in," and they'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not yet used to the fact that everyone hears what I say, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He is being brought through the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, in the statement that you signed and gave to the Court, you stated at paragraph 12 that the local SDS never had its own Crisis Staff. If I could refer you to tab 3 of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that is Exhibit P805, tab 2, and P836.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, you'll see that this document is the minutes of the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Sokolac held on 15 May 1992. And I'd like you to -- to refer you to the third paragraph. There's the heading "minutes," then there's a short paragraph which deals with the formal details. The second paragraph deals with the persons present. And if you could read the first sentence in the third paragraph, which reads as follows: "Before starting with the agenda Dragan Popovic informed the Crisis Staff about the meeting of the Municipal Board of the SDS Sokolac in which it was concluded that the Crisis Staff shall be comprised of 11 members," and it says "which" -- but may mean -- "whom are present today instead of 16 members." It is the case, isn't it, Mr. Bjelica that the Municipal Board of the SDS determined the constitution of the Crisis Staff of Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, yes. The Municipal Board of the Sokolac SDS did not have their staff, party staff but they delegated their representatives. When the SDS had representatives in the Municipal Assembly as deputies, there was only one Crisis Staff, Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Sokolac. And it is true that the Municipal Board asked Mr. Tupajic and the existing Crisis Staff that the number of members of the Crisis Staff be increased from 11 to 16, probably with a view of including a local director or managers of some institutions, such as the health centre and similar. So this is not in dispute. I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. If we could move on, I'd like to refer you to your statement again and also the evidence that you gave yesterday in quite some detail. And that was, effectively, you referred to a series of attacks on civilians, and in paragraph 18 of your statement you date various attacks from the 30th of June, 1992. And in paragraph 19 of your statement you say that as a result of these events, being those attacks against civilians, the VRS commenced various operations. The truth is, isn't it, Mr. Bjelica, that from early June 1992 the VRS was conducting offensive military operations along the corridor Pale-Sokolac-Vlasenica-Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify. What do you mean when you say "the corridor Pale-Sokolac-Vlasenica-Zvornik"? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the best way to do that is to refer Mr. Bjelica to three exhibits. The first one I'd like to deal with is at tab 6. And if that could have an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, this is a directive from Ratko Mladic dated 6th June 1992. And I'd like to refer you, first of all, to paragraph 4, and that appears in your copy on the first page. And the part of it I'd like to refer you to is the part with introductory words which are "I decided." And then the words as follows: "By using a part of our forces, implement offensive actions in order to mop up or cleanse the territories from the groups that stayed behind and from the individuals belonging to the enemy.
