Provide secure communication throughout the territory of Serbian Republic of BH as much as secure connections with FRY." Now, if you could turn over the page, I'd now like to refer you to the specific tasks that were given to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And in here you'll see the definition of the assignments given -- the definition of the corridor. And that is in page -- on page 3 of your version, and it's the paragraph in the middle of the page. And the part I'd like to refer you to is the last sentence. And these are assignments that are set by Mladic in order to achieve the objective that he described in paragraph 4. And the assignment of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. It's at --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: First of all, at item 4, did you follow me, the part that I read out to you initially was on page 1 and --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now I'm referring you to the third page, and I'm referring you to the paragraph in the middle of the page which commences with the words "Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." And I'm referring you to the last sentence of that paragraph. And it says this. It says: "Further deblock the communication Sarajevo, Trnovo, and Pale, Zlatiste. Securing the road from Gorazde, Rogatica, and Zepa." Then it says this, last sentence: "Secure the communication Sarajevo-Sokolac-Vlasenica. Establish stronger communication with East Bosnian Corps." And of course the East Bosnian Corps -- their area of operations was north, including the municipalities of Sekovici, Bratunac, and Zvornik in the Birac area. So that's the corridor that I'm referring to. And that corridor that ran from Pale through Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, from Zvornik to the Drina and ultimately to the FRY is the corridor that Mladic ordered on 6 June 1992 should be the area in which offensive military actions take place. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it should be. First of all, the Eastern Bosnia Corps did not cover -- what is this? I think they were stationed in Bijeljina, had to go to do with Bihac [as interpreted]. This is in Republika Srpska, the Eastern Bosnia Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: A subordinate brigade was the Birac Brigade, it must be my pronunciation. The Birac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, okay. You confused me a little. I thought you said "Bihac."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll state the question, and the question is simply this: That in accordance with this order offensive military operations were conducted along that corridor or that communication line, if you'd like to refer to it in that manner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In our area they were not conducted, not as far as Konjevic Polje, perhaps with a view of linking up with Yugoslavia near Konjevic Polje. The communication lines were cut off in Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac and Zvornik. Likewise, parts of Ilidza were cut off, as were a number of parts of Novo Sarajevo, where Serbs were the majority population, the area which was controlled by the forces of VRS because it was not safe to go across Trebevic but Tvrdinici. So probably in order to secure the communication lines for the parts of Sarajevo where Serbs were in majority, including Grbavica, Nedzarici, part of Ilidza, Novo Sarajevo and Trnovo, this order was issued and these actions were carried out as far as I can remember in the area of Zlatiste and Osmace in order to liberate that communication line and render it safe for passage of civilians, the military, and the equipment. So I think that it was with that objective in mind that this was carried out. I never saw any documents to that effect. I'm speaking from my memory and as a person who lived in the area. Nobody asked us whether this was necessary or not, but I know that after a while that communication line was safer, the one across Trebevic because up until that time the route via Tvrdinici was used. Those were bad roads, in poor condition, dirt roads. Even later, after that, the road was not entirely safe because of the constant activity of sniper shooting at the passing vehicles from Trebevic. There was also a lot of shelling, and quite a few people from Sokolac perished in the area, in that portion of the communication line I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, are you seeking all these details?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a certain moment, of course, you -- you may -- it's your own responsibility to use your time as good as you can. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I will intervene, as I have been doing to date in -- when you're giving further details than those which I've sought in my question. Now, to assist you with specifically the actions that were being conducted in your municipality, I have two further documents, and they are tabs 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if they could both be given numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 7, Your Honours, will be P1155; and tab 8, Your Honours, will be P1156.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, if you could first turn to tab 7, and this is an order the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And the portion I'm interested in is in paragraph 2 which appears as the second paragraph on the first page. And again, reflecting the order that you've just seen of Mladic, it again sets out that these operations are to be conducted along this axis. And the last sentence of paragraph 2 reads: "Further on to, unblock the Sarajevo-Trnovo and Pale-Zlatiste roads, and simultaneously secure Rogatica, Zepa and Gorazde axes, and the Sarajevo-Sokolac-Vlasenica road to establish firmer connection with the Eastern Bosnia Corps." And if I could just refer you to the top of the document, you'll see under the heading "Sarajevo Corps command," it says: "Strictly confidential number 10-74-44." And if we could refer to what has been given the number P1156, which is at tab 8, you will see now this document - if you could turn to tab 8 - is the order from the 2nd Motorised Brigade command based in Sokolac. And if you look at the introductory details in this order, you'll see the first paragraph refers to the implementation of the order 10-74-44, dated 7 June 1992. And again, if you look at paragraph 2 of this order, once again the order of Mladic is carried through and refers to providing security and establishing a connection with the East Bosnia Corps through the road Sarajevo-Sokolac-Vlasenica. Now you actually see this order of 8th June 1992 issued from the command in Sokolac. Do you now recall that offensive military actions ordered by the Main Staff of the VRS were conducted along that axis from early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, first there was the order of the Main Staff issued to the corps -- the corps command, and then the corps commands in turn issued orders to brigade commands, the command of the 2nd Motorised Brigade. I don't know who this was issued to, their subordinate units, I think. This is probably in relation with the order issued by the Main Staff. This is the first time that I'm looking at this document; I've never had an opportunity to see a document of this kind, to be frank. And a moment ago I tried to explain what I knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bjelica. But having seen these orders now and having seen that they were implemented, do you see that the military actions conducted by the VRS were commanded from the highest level and they were offensive actions along that corridor. Do you now understand the reason for the actions that you observed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I indicated a moment ago when the Presiding Judge instructed me to do so, I explained what I know of this issue. Once the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade informed the leadership of the municipality - and we're talking about the same period of time - that as many as 7.000 members of the Muslim forces from Olovo and Kladanj, which were active in the direction of Sokolac and a number of surrounding villages, that there was an imminent danger for Pale and Sokolac because Sokolac borders with Sarajevo, Gorazde, Kladanj, and also Zepa, partly with Srebrenica as well; I'm referring to the wooded area around Bature [phoen]. So there was a lot of fear whether this pressure would be eventually resisted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Unfortunately again the level of detail that you possess in relation to the actions that were taken is not the focus of my question because we're not talking about specific matters. We're talking about your statement where you said that there were actions initiated by the VRS, and what we're -- what I'm presenting to you is the series of orders which preceded those actions. And having seen those orders, do you now see why these offensive military actions were undertaken from early June 1992? In other words, you see that what you saw on the ground was being conducted pursuant to these orders. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I explained in my previous answer that there was an assessment on the part of intelligence services that these forces were on the move. And this is the reason why these activities subsequently took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. If I could move to another topic, and that's the issue of disarmament. In paragraph 14 of your statement, you stated that in the summer of 1992 the VRS issued a disarmament order, but no one acted on this request. If I could refer you to tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if that could be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 29, Your Honours, would be P1157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, this is a report dated 27 July 1992 from Zoran -- Captain Zoran Markovic and it's to the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade in Sokolac, and it sets out that on 27 July 1992 weapons were confiscated from the village of Novoseoci, a number of hunting guns, one carbine, and a number of pistols. And if I could refer you also to tab 12 which is related to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if that could have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 12, Your Honours, would be P1158.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This document at tab 12, Mr. Bjelica, is a report to the Main Staff dated the same date as P1157. And that reports the Main Staff -- if you look at the second part or the last paragraph referring to Novoseoci in paragraph 1, and it reports to the Main Staff that: "Arms and other lethal equipment were handed over by the Muslim population to the 2nd Romanija Brigade representatives in the village of Novoseoci," and it specifies where that village is. And it says that: "The handover was carried out according to the arrangement and it believes -- it's believed that all -- it's believed that all weapons were not handed over." And in that regard, Mr. Bjelica, I have yet one more document which will provide the complete picture as to what the situation was. And unfortunately now if I could refer you to tab 44. I say "unfortunately" because it's some distance from tab 12. It also should be helpful. Tab 44, do you have that there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if I could have a number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 44, Your Honours, will be P1159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is dated 28th July, the day after the weapons were handed over. And it's a report from Radislav Krstic, the commander of the 2nd Romanija Brigade, to the corps. And I'm referring to the last paragraph of that report and Lieutenant-Colonel Krstic states that: "Within this territory in the villages of Micivoda, Raktitnica, Kramer Selo, and Novoseoci, there is a certain number of extremists who are peaceful for now. They are not causing problems for the Serbian population, but were keeping them under control." So my -- after reading those documents that describe the handing over of the arms, do you see that, in fact, the village of Novoseoci did act on the request of the VRS to hand over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I mean, clearly I'm scanning these documents very quickly. The last document, in my submission, needs to be read by the witness in whole before he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not consider that to be the case. The question is very specific, it's about the village of Novoseoci. The rest of the document does not address it. If my learned friend wishes to address other issues in the document, then obviously he's welcome to it. He can do so in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look before ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bjelica was just indicating to me possibly he wanted to respond, but if you could just wait --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you have asked your question. I am not quite clear as to what I'm supposed to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If you could just wait --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could ask your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- for a second, I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for a second, Mr. Bjelica. Yes, I think it's fair that the witness reads the -- tab 44. Mr. Bjelica, could you just read the document under tab 44 in its entirety just to have a general impression of what the content is without, perhaps, trying to understand every and each single detail but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, please put the question to the witness. You've confronted him with quite some documents, so try to formulate your question as clearly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bjelica, you've read this last document. It could be that my learned friend wishes to ask you questions about other aspects of this document, but my request -- my question is limited to the last paragraph and limited to the issue of Novoseoci. And the fact is that the three documents you have seen, P1157, P1158, and P1159, demonstrate that, in fact, contrary to your understanding set out in your statement, that no one acted on the order for disarmament. Contrary to that statement, in fact, Novoseoci did hand in its weapons. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. With all due respect, we are talking about hunting weapons after all. Nobody made an issue of hunting weapons. However, military weapons, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, mines and explosive devices, that was not handed over. People had licenses for hunting weapons and pistols. As for the military armament, no, nothing was handed over. So we're talking about mines, explosive devices, and other military types of weapons -- at least that was the information that we received formally from the brigade command. True, some of the hunting rifles were handed over but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica, for that clarification. I'd now like to move on to the events that occurred at Novoseoci. And you told the Trial Chamber about a young man who committed suicide because of what happened at Novoseoci. And it's correct, isn't it, that this young man had been a soldier and Radislav Krstic was his commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And as you understand it from his father, he committed suicide because he was haunted by what he'd been ordered to do on that day in Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could refer you to tab 28 of the materials. That's tab 28. And, Mr. Bjelica, I'm referring to the report -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could have an exhibit number for --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 22nd of September, 1992, which is the date that the action we've referred to in Novoseoci occurred. And if I could refer you, Mr. Bjelica -- it's a report, just to give the details, from Commander Radislav Krstic to the Main Staff of the army and the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And if I could refer you, Mr. Bjelica, to paragraph 1(B), and you will see that the third sentence down - and that's on the first page of your document - states as follows, and that is: "Radislav Krstic reports that during the day the village of Novoseoci was ciscenje, cleansed or mopped up in Glasinacko Polje." Now, this report of Krstic is about the events at Novoseoci that we have been talking about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that this was addressed to the Main Staff of the RS army, so this is not in dispute, no, I mean what he is sending.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. If we could move on to -- now to tab 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if we could have an exhibit number for tab 45.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And -- and this is an approval issued by Commander Krstic, and it's to certify that Dragomir Bozic from the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade is able to transfer various materiels from Novoseoci to Sokolac and that they're going to be transferred to Sokolac. In the second sentence it says: "Until final moving into a house in Novoseoci which the above named has chosen for future living." The date of this approval is the 26th of September, 1992. Now, Mr. Bjelica, it's the case, isn't it, that following the cleansing of the village in Novoseoci, Serbs moved in to the vacated homes in that village?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust me, I've never been to Novoseoci. I heard that some of the property was damaged and I also heard that some people were still living there. I didn't hear anything about the details, but I did hear that some people had moved into some houses there. I don't know how this can be done. I don't know how this person by the name of Bozic can be given such an approval. It -- this really escapes me. I don't understand how this was possible, but it seems to be an authentic document. I -- but simply, this is something that I haven't heard before. This is the first time that I see a document to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, just if you can confirm my understanding, that is that there were 144 people in Novoseoci, according to the census of 1991, and they were all Muslims. Now, it's the case that all the Muslims left and the people that you're referring to who lived in that village after the 22nd of September, 1992, they were Serbs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anyone was there, then they must have been Serbs. No one else left the area. When this happened in Novoseoci, as far as I can remember, women, children, and elderly left for Sarajevo. And now we know what happened to the rest of the population. Muslims certainly did not stay, so if anyone could live there then they must have been Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. I'd like to turn to another topic, and that's a matter that you raised yesterday in the context of discussing the detention of Karan Saronjic and Karmen Konda and the process for the transfer and release of those detainees, and you'll remember that there was a list in correspondence from Velibor Ostojic where they were mentioned as persons who may be exchanged. And you said this, just to refresh your memory. You said: "The Sokolac municipality had its own commission, just like any other municipality, its commission for searching for and exchanging persons who were missing and prisoners of war, and the president was Dragan Podinic. And this was constitutional procedure according to the rules and regulations that were in force at the time." Now, the first question is this: Dragan Podinic, he was a member of the Crisis Staff, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the -- he either attended or he was a member. I don't know who the members were. It is possible that he attended the meetings of the Crisis Staff or he was instructed by the Crisis Staff. I can't be sure of that, but I'm sure that he attended most of the meetings and it is possible that he was the president of the Crisis Staff -- actually, a member of the Crisis Staff rather than president. I can't remember exactly. I know he attended meetings. I remember that he attended meetings. I don't know what his role was, whether he was the president of the commission or a member of the Crisis Staff. There were a lot of people in the Crisis Staff, executives, holders of various positions in various institutions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, my question is based on the documentation. In fact, we've seen documentation in which his name appears as being a member. But the one thing that you did say was that he was the president of the exchange commission at the municipality level. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He could have been the president of the Crisis Staff and the president of that commission for exchanges. I'm sure that he was the latter in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could refer you to tab 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I don't think it has a number yet. Tab 35 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has no description on your list. For the record, it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I believe there is no translation in the tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- And we have the translation here. It's correspondence from the Sokolac municipality, prisoner of war exchange committee, addressed to the Army of Republika Srpska Committee for Exchange and its president Dragan Bulajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: First, Mr. Bjelica, if you could refer to this document which is, as I described, it's a 9 November 1992 communication from the exchange committee of Sokolac to the military exchange committee. And if you could look at the last page, and you'll see that it's signed by the president of the Sokolac committee, Dragan P., and can you confirm that that's a reference to Dragan Podinic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Podinic, the president of the army. I believe that the second person was Zoran Markovic and the chief of police, Predrag Krsmanovic. Those three members were members of the commission, the army, the police, and the court. Podinic was the president of the basic court in Sokolac. Zoran Markovic I believe is the second name, I'm not 100 per cent sure, he could have been the representative of the military. He worked in the security organ. And the third person, the third member, Predrag Krsmanovic, the chief of the Sokolac police. Those are the three members who signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. If I could refer you to the first page and there is a list of prisoners who are put at the disposal of this military commission. And can you confirm that it was part of Mr. Podinic's role to maintain lists of the detainees in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to have lists to know who the detainees were. If somebody was in charge of the missing persons or the prisoners, then had to consult the list to see whether they had been kept by a unit or in an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And we have looked at various statements of the persons listed here and other statements referring to them. These people were detained from around late summer 1992, first of all, in the Sokolac primary school; and secondly, around September 1992, transferred to the school in the village of Cavarine. At some stage in early 1993 most of them were transferred to Vogosca --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cavarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Cavarine. Is that consistent with your knowledge as to the places that the people were detained in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a certain number of persons whose names I never knew were kept in the primary school in Sokolac, Cavarine, and in the third place called Knezina, but I'm not sure about the third place. And I believe that they were kept there for a while. Those were Muslims, but they -- those were military prisons and they were also used for Serbs. And most often it was the Serbs and the Muslims who were there together. Even two Serb executives were kept there for some disciplinary issues. They either failed to return to their units or they had deserted. And that's why they were brought in. So it was not just the Muslims who were detained but also the Serbs. I'm not saying that these people were not there. I know some of the Muslims, I don't know who they were by name, but I'm sure that they were taken there and that they were kept in designated facilities that were designated for that person by the security organs. Both Serbs and Muslims, and there's nothing disputable about that, and this was signed by the commission for the exchanges, and this document is valid, a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, you say "both Serbs and Muslims." Now, the information that we have is that -- well, I'm not in possession of any information about Serb detainees. But nonetheless, if we accept there were some Serb detainees, the vast majority of the detainees were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was not the case, but the Serbs could not be on the list because nobody was looking for them, they were not to be exchanged. They hailed from Sokolac, Pale, Rogatica, that's where they resided. Their families knew where they were. I'm not disputing anything, but I can say that there were a lot more Serbs there than Muslims for various disciplinary offences. There is information on who was taken in, who was punished. I'm sure you will find that in the files of the army of the defence ministry and other archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Podinic did possess that information as to who was taken in, the circumstances in which they were taken in, and the results of any interrogations that may have been conducted and the length of the person's detention. He was in possession of that information, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have that at his disposal because the investigations in this case were conducted by the military investigative bodies, and Podinic could only have information. And if somebody searched for certain people, Podinic would then send a request to the brigade command to see whether the latter had information as to what the case may have been with those people who were searched by somebody. And if the feedback was positive, and it was only a matter of their goodwill whether they would provide the commission with the information, then Podinic would inform a commission at a higher level that was in charge of the exchanges that the person in question had been located and where they could be found. As for the investigations, I'm sure that he did not have information about any investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that information would have been held by the investigating bodies; namely, the police and the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about military conscripts or officers, then it would just be the military security, not the police. The two were separate. If the person in question was a war prisoner, they would conduct interviews and then they would inform whoever. I don't know the procedure. I'm not privy to the procedure, but I know there was a procedure in place as to how these investigations and interviews were conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, it's the case, according to our information, that most, if not all, of the people that are listed here, that's the first 18 people, were civilians not combatants. And is that consistent with your knowledge that a large number of civilians were detained in these places?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you're saying that I said a lot of civilians were detained. It says here that they were prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't say that. There must have been a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Your Honour. In my submission, and it's an unfortunate term of phrase that Mr. Margetts has used on two occasions, "According to our information." If he wants to put his case, and I encourage him to do that, but he should avoid using that expression. He should put the case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure I agree with my learned friend, but I don't have much time, so I will proceed and I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Matter resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if I could do that by referring to tab 40 -- sorry, an extra document, or is that tab -- it is tab -- it is at the document at tab 46, and if that could have an exhibit number. The translation is being distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 46, Your Honours, will be P1163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, if you look at number 8 on the previous document, the document that was at tab 35, you'll see that that's a woman who was detained. It's Sema Mujanovic. And what I've now provided to you which is P1163 is --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page am I supposed to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the first page of the 9 November 1992 document, which is at tab 35, there is a person listed at number 8, and it's a woman by the name of Sema Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't a clue, believe me. I don't know whether her name was Sema, whether she was a female. I haven't a clue. Everything is possible, but I don't really want to go into --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's the reason I've presented to you the next document, which is P1163, and you'll see this is a statement given in January 1993 by Sema Mujanovic. And she describes -- first of all, she describes that she's a housewife born on the 5th of May, 1930, in the village of Knezina and accordingly she would have been 62 years old at the time of her listing on this exchange document. And she describes the fact that she was taken from the village Sahbegovici and she was detained in the prison in the primary school, and she provides other details. But the reason I present that to you is to ask you this question and put it to you that in fact the Muslims detained in these facilities we've described, they were not POWs but they were civilians, and Mrs. Sema Mujanovic is an example of that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I can't confirm this. I never heard of any of these people or most of them. I don't know whether they had been armed. I don't know what is at stake. I really can't be a judge of that. I haven't a clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure what time we will take a break, if we will take one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take one more break. We -- since we had a late start -- could you tell me how much time you would still need? That could be of importance from a scheduling ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously, depending on the answers, but I think half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could go a little bit longer now, then I would have a better idea, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue for a while and then we'll see in some 20 minutes where we stand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you gave evidence about the Presidency of the Republika Srpska. You never attended a session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, in the context of the video that you were shown of the funeral that took place in December 1991, you mentioned the relationship between the JNA organs and the attitudes of the Serbian people. And in that context I'd like you now to refer to tab 1 which is an intercept of 13 December 1991 between yourself and Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that has -- that has an exhibit number of sorts. It's P64A, and I will attempt to get to you the footnote and binder number. But it's an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Bjelica on 13 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, it's a short conversation so I would invite you to read the full conversation.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, you refer to the fact that there were -- you say to Mr. Karadzic when he asks you to deploy units under the command of Milosevic for combat in Slavonia you say to him: "We have two units up there." And that's the case, that these were units that the party had formed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this conversation transpired after Mr. Karadzic wanted to talk to Mr. Tupajic, the president of the municipality. Mr. Karadzic wanted to talk to him but could not locate him in his office. Mr. Tupajic and I were in the SDS office at the moment, and then Mr. Karadzic left a message with the secretary for him to get back to him, for Mr. Tupajic to get back to him, and if Mr. Tupajic couldn't do it, then I was supposed to get back to him. Since we were together in the office, we were there, the two of us together, and I was the one who actually returned the calls for Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So my question simply -- it actually isn't important for our purposes to have the details of what transpired on the day. It's just that the two units you referred to, they were units formed by the SDS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. SDS -- the SDS did not form a single unit. This was the regular JNA, and those units were under the command of Colonel Milosevic, Dragomir. And the Chief of Staff was Mr. Asim Dzambasovic. Dzambasovic took the unit towards the end of 1991 to Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, Mr. Bjelica. The Court has in fact heard evidence from Mr. Dzambasovic, so I'm not interested in these further details. What I'd like to move on to you then -- Mr. Karadzic then says: "You should find Rajko Dukic to send a company from Milici." And then he says to you: "They have all that formed. They have it formed down there." And it's the case that in Milici the SDS had formed units and, in fact, around about the date of this intercept, within a few days, they had a parade in Milici where about 400 men were gathered and they celebrated the formation of those units. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that this was the SDS. This was organised by the municipality of Milici, not the SDS. I can't see anywhere that the SDS did that. The SDS was in power, so everything can be ascribed to the SDS as a political organisation because it had power and it did whatever it did through legal institutions. But it wasn't the SDS who did that. This was done according to the prevailing need, and here Mr. Karadzic doesn't tell me: See what you can do. He says: First see how you can replenish the units because there was a lot of desertion. You should see how you to replenish units through the military department. The Territorial Defence was in charge of replenishing the units that were sent anywhere. An appeal was to be sent to conscripts to respond to the call-ups in order to be able to form these two units. It was nothing that was apart from the legitimate and legal institutions that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, to assist you with the details here, I'd like to refer you to tab 31 which is a -- which already has an exhibit number, which is P64A and P259. And I can now assist with the exhibit number for the intercept at tab 1, and that is P64A, binder 5, footnote 82. And this intercept, you'll see, Mr. Bjelica, is an intercept that describes the nature of the units that were formed in Milici, those units you were referring to in your conversation with Mr. Karadzic. This is a conversation that Zvonko Bajagic of Milici has with Radovan Karadzic, whilst Mr. Koljevic is present with Karadzic. Now, the substance of the discussion is that Bajagic communicates to Mr. Karadzic that they formed -- in two days they've recruited about 600 volunteers. And he says: "They are all trained and armed." And that's at the bottom of the English on the first page, and it is -- it is at the bottom of the B/C/S and top of -- B/C/S page 1 and the top of the B/C/S page 2. And that's the case, isn't it, that Bajagic and Dukic had formed units of that strength and they trained them and they'd armed them and that was an activity of the SDS, and that's why the report is going to the president of the party, Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion that was billeted in Milici was based on the 216th Mountain Brigade based in Han Pijesak. The person who had been sent by the brigade from the command was Major Grajic, and he was sent to establish the battalion because a lot of people had deserted. I'm talking about Muslims who had deserted the battalion in Vlasenica. Now why Mr. Bajagic is saying this, I don't know, but I know this was a legal and legitimate battalion who was -- which was on the strength of the 216th Mountain Brigade, and General Rado -- Colonel Milosevic was directly in charge of the establishment of that unit. And Dzambasovic and him sent Major Grajic to carry out the establishment and replenishment of that unit. There may have been people who wanted to gain political points for that, but I'm sure what I'm saying and I'm sure that your analysis will eventually demonstrate that, that this was a legal and legitimate unit of the 216th Mountain Brigade, the command of which was in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned legality in your answer, the previous answer, and you emphasised with some strength when reviewing the video of the funeral that -- the fact that at that funeral there were no nationalist symbols. The only flag displayed was the Yugoslav flag and the only symbols were that of the JNA. And I'd like to draw your attention to the comments of Mr. Bejagic where he informs Mr. Karadzic that the parade they intend to hold will not only display the Yugoslav flag but, he says: "Tomorrow we are going to hold the Serbian flag alongside the other one." And Mr. Karadzic acknowledges that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, read out what Karadzic's response is, please, and what Bejagic says thereafter. It's rather important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you're invited to give the context to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll see that, Mr. Bjelica, on the third page of the intercept. And I'll read out the exchange. Karadzic -- they're talking about whether or not a representative of the party can attend this rally. And Karadzic says: "Maybe state body, state body, yes, but it would not" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the third page English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Second page English, sorry, Your Honours. And it's at the bottom of the second page of the English, and it's the third page at the top for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have problems anyhow because all pages are numbers 5 out of 5, which is not very helpful if you want to find your page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Apologies for that error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've now found it. Please read it in its entirety the relevant portion to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Karadzic says: "Maybe state bodies, state body. Yes, but it would not be good to send a party body." Bejagic says: "But army wants it. Tomorrow we are going to hold Serbian flag alongside the other one." Karadzic says: "And Yugoslav?" And Bejagic says: "Precise. The army is not concerned about the symbols. This is clearly" -- Karadzic says: "Uh-huh." And Bejagic continues what he was saying. He's saying: "This is clearly patriotic Serb army. This was not organised by JNA or anybody else." So Bejagic, that's our submission and on the face of this text, Bejagic makes it clear that it's a patriotic Serb army who are not concerned about flying the Serb flag. And he states quite clearly: "We are going to hold the Serbian flag at this rally." And that's the case, isn't it, that these units were organised by the SDS and they considered themselves patriotic Serb units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot accept that. This is not correct. Those units were organised by the JNA. The SDS was engaged in a political propaganda. They motivated -- tried to motivate people and appeal to able-bodied men because Muslims had refused to join the JNA, which at the time was the only legal and legitimate military formation in the area of Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Yugoslavia, generally speaking. So now some say that those were SDS units. It is true that the SDS made the request to that effect because SDS fought for Yugoslavia. This can be seen from the video that was shown yesterday. Only Yugoslavia was mentioned, not Serbia, Serbdom, or Greater Serbia, which was never mentioned at all. So we're talking about the regular unit, that is, the 216th Brigade of the Yugoslavia army. You're now mentioning Bejagic. Bejagic was not a member of any body. He did not have any function. I don't see the reason why a conversation with him is here deemed relevant. I don't know that he had any official formal function whatsoever at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But it's the case that the -- this formation of units and the deployment of the units was none of the legitimate business of the president of the SDS, Radovan Karadzic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is true officers relied on Mr. Karadzic as the leader of the Serbs because the SDS, the leadership of the SDS, was the only one who publicly declared their positions, that is, that they were fighting for the preservation of Yugoslavia and the preservation of the Yugoslav People's Army. The representatives of the SDA and HDZ called upon members of their community not to respond to the call-up papers for the JNA. So Dr. Karadzic, Nikola Koljevic, and Biljana Plavsic were actually appealing to Serbs to respond, because Serbs saw their protection and their salvation in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have about five minutes of examination left. If Your Honour would like to take -- if we could take a break now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be better to continue for another five minutes if the interpreters are able to assist us for the next five minutes, then have a break. Then, Mr. Josse, there will be an opportunity for re-examination and we'll see whether the approximate two Judges have any additional questions. Because we -- since we started late we are finishing late as well. This was announced so that we are compensated for the first half-hour we lost. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bjelica, yesterday your response to the government of Republika Srpska in relation to the document known as the Variant A and B document was referred to. And His Honour, the President of the Court, informed you that the Chamber had received evidence that reference to the document had been made in official settings and he mentioned the Assembly. Now, there was a meeting on the 14th of February, 1992 at the Holiday Inn where Radovan Karadzic called for activation of the second level of the Variant A and B instructions. And I'd like to refer you to tab 47 and the translation's here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And this document is part of a -- is part of P64A, and again I'll attempt to get the more precise reference in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Particular page that I'm referring you to, Mr. Bjelica -- the particular page is marked with eight symbols at the top, SAO3016. And this confirms that the deputy from the Sokolac, Marko Simic, was present at the Holiday Inn on the 14th of February, 1992. Now, Mr. Bjelica, it's the case, isn't it, that in fact the Variant A and B instructions were simply, as it appears on their face, party instructions and that on the 14th of February, 1992, Marko Simic attended the Holiday Inn. He received further information from the party president as to how these instructions were to be implemented, and he returned to Sokolac. And he informed the members -- the leading people, including yourself, of what was required to further implement these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You may be asked further questions about this in re-examination. If you have something very brief you would like to state now, do so, but there's no need for any lengthy response.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything to say because Marko Simic never handed me over anything, nor did he ever explain anything to me. I have never seen the document. The document was never seen by anyone in our area. I believe that Tupajic testified here, and others as well, and I don't think that this document was seen by any of them. Milan Tupajic was the one who would have got this document, but he didn't, nor did I get it. And I never heard of the existence of this document; I'm referring to Variant A and B. This is something entirely new to me. I never heard anything about the existence of such a document. At any meeting Mr. Simic never gave me anything. It is true that he travelled from Sokolac, he was a deputy after all, and he probably spent a night at the Holiday Inn hotel. He may have had company there, so he probably stayed on for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Bjelica, it's our case that you did receive it, and it's our case that the letter you wrote and the explanation you've provided in relation to this document has no substance at all. And whilst it may demonstrate loyalty to the party to continue to deny the document, as you must be now aware, the overwhelming evidence you will have seen watching the various trials before this Trial Chamber mean that that denial is now of no assistance to your party. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, I mean, that it would be of no assistance to our party, but I aside by what I said. The organisation of the party was in the hand of the Executive Board and the Main Board, and it all remained there at the Holiday Inn hotel. This issue, the issue of two variants, was never discussed, never debated, at any level, at any meeting. And once again, all of these documents were published. They can be found in the archives of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They took them all. They published all these documents, and they would have probably published that one -- this one as well if it had indeed existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica. The document that I referred to as P64A, being the Holiday Inn receipt in relation to Mr. Simic is binder 11 footnote 188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'll noticed that you provided us with a translation. It may have been an easy task for the translators since the firm -- the Holiday Inn puts everything in English on it as well. I was a bit surprised that even you did not translate the back the English into B/C/S which would, of course, have been the ultimate perfectionism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one and only document hat was not in need of being translated, at least as far as what has been translated, the translation was provided very quickly. The Chamber wonders whether the other translations will arrive as quickly as well. Did you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I have one further question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. Then that's the very last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, you've described in your evidence the tensions between the ethnic communities in Bosnia. And it's a fact, isn't it, that you have advocated and you continue to advocate separation between the Serbs and the Muslims, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could refer you, Mr. Bjelica, to tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if that could be given an exhibit number --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, isn't he entitled to say a little bit more than that? He was about to. Before he sees the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In fairness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was about to do that. I heard him say "no" and not much else. But, Mr. Bjelica, if you would like to add anything to that where you said that you did not advocate and that you do not continue to advocate separation between the Serbs and the Muslims, could you -- before looking at the document, Mr. Bjelica. Before looking at the document. Mr. Bjelica. Yes, I understand, you do not know who is addressing you because you hear it all through the interpreters. Could you explain? You said "no." Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you advocated or -- and continue to advocate separation between the Serbs and the Muslims. You said simply "no." Mr. Josse had the impression that you'd like to add something to that, although a simple no is a clear answer. But if you'd like to add something, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are reasons for me saying that. We fought for Yugoslavia. We wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to remain within Yugoslavia. When we realised that it was all to no avail, that this was not accepted by the representatives of the other two communities, Muslims and Croats, then as a compromise we accepted the Dayton Bosnia-Herzegovina, compromised of two entities. If Dayton Accords were to be called into question and if the pressure on Republika Srpska continued, then we would raise the issue again. However, once the Serbs accept something then they abide by it completely. I fully support the Dayton Accords, that is, Bosnia and Herzegovina made up of two entities where three communities live together. This is what I accepted and this is what I am not giving up. If we were to engage in out-voting once again and have the same situation as it prevailed in 1992, then Serbs would be again in a difficult position and would again -- and would advocate an independent republic. Nothing should happen, nothing should be happening, in Bosnia and Herzegovina without the consent of the two entities and the three constitutional communities or peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, if I just may -- you say, "Well, we accept the Dayton Accord." Of course the Dayton Accord includes this administrative separation between Republika Srpska and the other entity, but the Dayton Accord does not say, as far as I'm aware - and please correct me when I'm wrong - that human beings should separated, Muslims not living together with Serbs, or Croats not living together with Muslims. It doesn't say anything about that, isn't it? It's -- even goes rather in the direction of giving an opportunity to go back to where you come from or to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dayton Accord became acceptable and convenient for all. None of the communities -- no community can feel endangered and threatened. As Serbs have the same rights in the federation as other peoples have in Republika Srpska. I'm talking about two entities. I know that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a state today, that is true, but we are talking about two administrative units within that state: The Federation and Republika Srpska. And I fully respect and support the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, your support for the Dayton Accords is certainly not recognised by Lord Ashdown, is it? He considers you to be someone who is destroying the rule of law in Bosnia and conducting yourself in a way inimicable to the implementation of the Dayton Accords. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep it short. Lord Ashdown says that you are conducting yourself in a way not in accordance with the Dayton Agreements. Any comment on that? First of all, do you know that, that this is the position taken by Lord Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this was his opinion. In the introductory part I mentioned the reasons why, but this is not justified. I'm convinced that this would be corrected and cleared up in the next following days when talking about the suspicion that was cast upon me, and not only myself but a number of other individuals who were sanctioned. I assure you that there's nothing in it, and I'm sure that the future will show that I'm right. We're talking about political gains and political interests of certain individuals. I'm not responsible for this. I am once again in favour, entirely in favour, of the Dayton Accords and the respect of the three constitutive peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I never tried to apply for citizenship --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is my final question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I would just like you, Mr. Bjelica, to read a portion of the article which is before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, it's on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could have an exhibit number, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: P1164 is an article published in the Washington Post, and it's written by Daniel Williams, and it's dated the 26th of July, 2004, and it quotes Mr. Bjelica. And I would just like Mr. Bjelica --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: First of all, the part I'm referring to is on page 3 of 3. You'll see in the middle of the page there's a paragraph starts about the word "Ashdown." Following that paragraph, there is a paragraph starting with the name "Bjelica." And then a paragraph starting with the words "Serbs fled." It's the two paragraphs, the one starting with the name "Bjelica" and the one starting with the words "Serbs fled" that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And for your information, Mr. Bjelica, it is on the second page of what is a partial translation of the article. And it's the two -- the second and the third paragraph on that translation, Mr. Bjelica, that I'd like you to read. The first paragraph refers to the fact that you were organising an expansion of the Sokolac cemetery to accommodate bodies of Serbs brought from Sarajevo. And this is what you said, Mr. Bjelica, you said: "Serbs fled that" -- well, the commentator says: "Serbs fled that city by the thousands after war ended." And you say: "We wanted to have a complete break from the Muslims. We do not want to live with them and we don't want to be buried near them."

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is taken out of context. This is not an integral conversation. This was recorded by a camera. I remember this clearly. There was a woman whose husband and two sons had been killed, and it was in that context that I said that everything that happened they did not want to live next to each other. And that is why the dead were transferred from Sarajevo. I did not expand cemeteries. They were expanded because of the circumstances. And the property were transferred after the signing of the Dayton Accords. Although the Municipal Assembly of Sarajevo reached a declaration on the stay of the Serbs in Sarajevo, they advocated further attempts at talks and that Sarajevo should be organised in districts and apply a model similar to Washington, or to Belgium, that the same model should be applied here. But they simply could not be convinced, and that is why they took out 1.000 of their dead to Sokolac. They even re-buried the dead who had died years ago and transferred them elsewhere. They were not interested in their property. Your Honours, I assure you, this was all done during that period of time in April -- from January to April and later in -- but at any rate in the winter, where temperatures are very low, minus -- up to minus 30. There was nothing that could be done about it. They could not be stopped. That was the decision of the main leaders from the republic, because the leadership of the Republika Srpska was accused of having handed over Sarajevo at the table, of having betrayed Sarajevo. The idea of district was agreed upon. However, later on, Milosevic gave up the idea, although the same idea was proposed in the Cutileiro Plan advocated by Izetbegovic. After the signing of the Cutileiro Plan, we could read in the papers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't get the title quoted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is an emotional -- this was an emotional conversation that took place at the military cemetery. You have to bear in mind the context. I apologise for speaking into greater detail, but you need to know the context. This was happening at the military cemetery in the presence of the mothers who had lost their sons and their husbands. The woman here was talking about how she had lost everyone and how she could no longer go on living together with them. So this should not be taken out of context. This doesn't affect what was agreed upon in Washington by our leadership. And whatever was agreed upon by the three communities is binding for me and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Bjelica. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Bjelica, we'll have a break. Perhaps you -- could the witness be led out of the courtroom so that we look at time issues. Yes. Could you lead Mr. Bjelica out of the courtroom. Mr. Josse, how much time would you think you would need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. Then -- yes, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could have a break now of 20 or 25 minutes and then have that five minutes' re-examination. But I'm looking at the interpreters and the technicians, also for tapes. We also could see whether re-examination could take place immediately. If it's five minutes, Mr. Margetts, I don't think that you would need much time after that, certainly not after the questions of the Judges because the Judges have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that sounds appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- I don't know whether it's still possible to get Mr. Bjelica back into the courtroom at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before, I'm not used yet that everyone listened to what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the procedural matter, to do with the letter, that presumably does not now need to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can tell you something about it; it takes 30 seconds. We were informed that the relevant portion of the newspaper appears in the letter written by Mr. Krajisnik. So the translation of the letter, and it is available for you now, Mr. Josse, for inspection -- at least the suggestion is that there would be no need to have any further translation of the newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's being translated in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll have the weekend to consider it with Mr. Krajisnik, will I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that we'll not take any action before the weekend so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik is indicating he's happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the envelope will be returned to you at this moment -- after this session by the -- or do we have it now -- I have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter remains in the hands of Mr. Registrar. You'll receive a copy of the B/C/S original and the English translation, Mr. Josse, and we'll hear from you next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, since Mr. Josse announced that he would need only a couple of minutes for further questions, we decided not to have a break and finish now. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab 16, please, P1153.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This relates to page 34 of today's transcript for the Court's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm informed that possibly the reference is to the Prosecution exhibits. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, let's at least try to have the -- tab 16, Prosecution bundle. Yes -- May I inform the parties that where earlier I asked myself whether the interpreters and technicians would agree, it now turns out that we have only six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Wrong bundle. I'm grateful to Mr. Margetts. Wrong bundle. It's my fault. I didn't make the position clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that -- I asked interpreters and technicians whether we could do -- if you can do it in six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Defence would be anxious to get out of this courtroom early as well today, but -- but, I don't want to put myself under that sort of pressure. On balance, I think we should take the break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the tape, if it runs out, then we have no transcript of the session anymore. Would we then agree that we would have the -- well, a relatively short break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Short as possible, I'm happy to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that we would re-start at 2.00 sharp and not spend more than 10 to 12 minutes from that. Yes, we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, please proceed, and the apologies from the Chamber for knowing that you would like to start as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, we've altered our plans and we are no longer in a great rush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I'm not going to take very long. I can assure everyone of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, I wanted you to look at tab 16 of the Prosecution bundle, P1153. And as I've already indicated your evidence, as far as this is concerned, is found at page 34 -- no, that's not a reference you. Just that page, for you, please, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, you do. Is that the page that you have open in front of you, the extracts from the Glas newspaper. That's the English. I want you to look at the original. Do you remember, it's the article in the bottom right-hand corner or just above the bottom right-hand corner, which says "Sarajevo, 4th of March," and it's -- have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked about the document. You were asked about its contents, and you said: "I don't remember this." You were then asked in turn whether the Serb people of the SAO Romanija had lost confidence in the possibility of a political agreement with the Muslims, and you said "yes." On what basis did you give that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the killing of the wedding party member, Mr. Gardovic, and everything that happened around that time and as -- as a result of violent behaviour of the Muslim Assemblymen in the National Assembly, they didn't send the request to the Council for the Equality of Peoples and National Minorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the referendum was organised for an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, what else could the Serbs do? The Serbs couldn't do anything else. Not a single request, not a single position of the Serbs was ever taken into account. On the day of the referendum, this man in the wedding party was killed. They torched the Serb flag. What could we expect under such government of Mr. Izetbegovic and likes of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm going to move on. You were asked at the end of cross-examination by my learned friend Mr. Margetts about your views on ethnic division. When you were its president, what did the Municipal Assembly of Serb Sarajevo say to the inhabitants of the old city of Sarajevo in relation to whether or not they should leave that city?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN BJELICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time this Assembly passed a declaration. According to that declaration, the Serbs were to remain in Sarajevo. They were not to move. Our politicians, including the president of the National Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, launched an appeal of the Assembly of the Serb Sarajevo to the Serbs not to move out of Sarajevo but, rather, to build their own Sarajevo. Those were the messages and those were honest and sincere positions. However, nobody could convince the Serbs from Ilidza, Vogosca, Rajlovac, Hadzici, Ilijas, Grbavica and other parts of Sarajevo where Serbs formed a majority and which were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska and which were parts of Republika Srpska to remain an integral part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina because nobody trusted Mr. Izetbegovic and the extremists from the SDA. In other words, the town assembly adopted the declaration, it publicised it, it sent it to the population of all these municipalities asking them not to move out but, rather, to remain, to stay put, to go on living in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelica, since the Chamber has no further questions to you either, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague in circumstances that are not very comfortable for you, not very pleasant for you; at the same time, they exist. Nevertheless, thank you very much for coming, for answering questions from both the parties and from the Bench, and I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again, but since you are accompanied, I take it that your safety is guaranteed, Mr. Bjelica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have nothing to say. Everything was correct. My accommodation was correct. People were correct there. I don't have a single objection to anything, regardless of the situation that I am in. And I would like to thank you for the correctness extended towards me in the situation that I'm facing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm pleased to hear that. Thank you very much. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, we'll not at this moment deal with the exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: By saying that, as far as Prosecution exhibits are concerned, I object to none of them, save P1163, which I am going to object to as strongly as I can, and I can deal that at any convenient time next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's already on the record, 1163. Strong -- not only an objection, but a strong objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. If my learned friend could give me notice if when he's going to take objection to any exhibits. During the course of the afternoon by e-mail would be fine. I would be grateful for the same courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll provide an e-mail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Because we have now Prosecution Exhibits 1149 and 1152 up till and including 1164, objections on 1163. Defence exhibits 162 up to and including D168. Some descriptions have still to be finalised, so I'll not give a decision at this very moment, apart from that 1163 would need more time, anyhow, I take it for the -- your objections as such. All the documents first have to be checked by Mr. Registrar, translations, their descriptions, et cetera. So we'll deal with -- finally deal with it either Monday or Tuesday, because we'll resume, once we have adjourned on next Monday at 9.00 in Courtroom I, but I also would like to announce to the parties that the Chamber intends - and we hope we can finish it in time - to file this afternoon a very short decision to which is attached the rules of procedure for Chamber witnesses which we may call, as we said before. We would start already preparations because otherwise we would be too late, although a final decision on whether or not to call those witnesses will be taken at the end of the Defence case. But you're invited to give any comments on the procedure attached to it by next Tuesday during the time available for procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So we'll have an opportunity to make oral submissions on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm drawing your attention to it now that you don't miss it and only find out Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until next Monday morning, 9.00, Courtroom I.
